During the first stage, participants completed the task either with or without access to ChatGPT, while performance incentives were independently manipulated.

table.text: An additional control condition was included in which participants completed an alternative first-stage task without genAI assistance or motivational incentives.
Participants were randomly assigned to the experimental conditions using block randomisation.
Participants were recruited through printed posters, mailing lists, and paid advertisements on Facebook and Instagram targeting adult residents of the city in which the laboratory was located.
An additional four participants were excluded according to pre-registered criteria, because they failed to answer at least two of the three attention-check questions correctly.
These questions were designed to assess whether participants had attended to the presented material.
The final sample consisted of 193 participants: 128 women, 61 men, and four participants who did not specify their gender.
Consequently, participants had to construct and retain a structured representation of the network and derive conclusions that were not stated explicitly in the presented descriptions.
In the first stage, participants were presented with subsets of statements describing relatively small sections of the network.
This procedure was consistent with cognitive load theory, as it reduced the number of interacting elements that participants had to process simultaneously.
In the second stage, participants completed a more comprehensive reasoning task involving a substantially larger portion of the network.
Participants had access to additional paper-based materials with 20 information points, each containing one or two statements.
In the third stage, participants completed a 10-item memory test assessing their retention of information presented in both Stage 1 and Stage 2.
In SymSpan, participants had to remember locations of red squares in a 4 × 4 grid of potential locations.
After each item, a distractor task was presented, where participants were asked to judge symmetry of a displayed shape along its vertical axis.
In OSpan, participants had to remember a series of letters presented one at a time, with the letters randomly selected for each trial.
After each letter, participants had to solve a simple maths problem as a distractor task.
At the end of the block participants were asked to recall the letters in the correct order.
Additionally, participants provided information about the frequency of use of genAI tools and the type of tools they use.
Participants were tested in a computer laboratory, with up to two participants taking part simultaneously at separate workstations.
Upon arrival, participants were asked to switch off their mobile phones or activate airplane mode.
They then received information about the study, provided written informed consent, and were assigned a pseudonymised participant code.
Before the reasoning task, participants assigned to the incentive condition received standardised information intended to increase the perceived importance of their performance.
In the genAIassistance condition, ChatGPT was available on a separate monitor and participants were informed that they could use it freely to support their performance on the task.

Participants assigned to the control group showed numerically lower Stage 2 accuracy (𝑀 = 57.3%, 𝑆𝐷 = 17.9%) than participants in the comparable experimental condition with no genAI access and no incentives (𝑀 = 64.1%, 𝑆𝐷 = 15.2%).

Further, the effect of incentives was significant among participants without genAI access, such that participants completed the task more slowly when additional incentives were provided (EMM = 54.30; 95%CI[44.03; 66.28]) than when no additional incentives were provided (EMM = 39.00; 95%CI [31.04; 48.40]; estimate = -0.216, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.060, 𝑡(153) = -3.584, 𝑝 < .001).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: The impact of cognitive support on the effectiveness of solving tasks
table.research_questions:
We will test the following hypotheses:

Hypothesis 1a (Offloading Advantage):
Participants with access to gAI assistance during the chunked reasoning task (stage 1) will perform better (higher accuracy) in the subsequent extended reasoning task (stage 2) than those without assistance.

Hypothesis 1b (Relational Knowledge Advantage):
Participants without gAI assistance during the chunked reasoning phase (stage 1) will perform better (higher accuracy) in the extended reasoning task (stage 2) than those with assistance.

Hypothesis 1c (Knowledge building vs Cognitive fatigue):
Participants in the control condition (without gAI assistance and with an alternative pseudoword chunked reasoning task in stage 1) will perform worse on the extended reasoning task (stage 2) and on the memory task (stage 3), compared to no gAI assistance experimental group which experiences a similar level of cognitive fatigue.

Hypothesis 2a (Speed via Offloading):
Participants with gAI assistance during the chunked reasoning phase (stage 1) will complete the extended reasoning task (stage 2) faster than those without assistance.

Hypothesis 2b (Speed via Internalization):
Participants without gAI assistance during the chunked reasoning phase (stage 1) will complete the extended reasoning task (stage 2) faster than those with assistance.

Hypothesis 3 (Motivation Advantage on accuracy)
We predict a main effect of motivation on performance in stage 2, whereby participants in the high motivation condition (with additional incentives) will demonstrate better accuracy. We will also examine an interaction between motivation and gAI assistance (see H1) on an exploratory basis.

Hypothesis 4 (Motivation Advantage on speed)
We predict a main effect of motivation on performance in stage 2, whereby speed of completion will be different for participants in the high motivation condition and low motivation condition. We will also examine an interaction between motivation and gAI assistance (see H2) on an exploratory basis.

Hypothesis 5 (Memory Internalization Advantage):
We predict a main effect of gAI assistance on memory performance in stage 3, whereby memory will be enhanced for participants without gAI assistance, as well as a main effect of motivation on memory performance in stage 3, whereby participants in the high motivation condition will demonstrate better memory for the pseudoword network. We will also examine an interaction between the two on an exploratory basis.

Hypothesis 6 (Cognitive Offloading Behaviour):
Within the gAI assistance condition, participants in the low motivation condition (no additional incentives) will engage in more cognitive offloading (i.e., more gAI requests) than those in the high motivation condition.

Hypothesis 7 (Offloading Modulated by Working Memory Capacity):
Participants in gAI assistance condition with lower working memory capacity will make more use of gAI assistance (i.e. more gAI requests) than those with higher working memory capacity.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview:
The study will include a 2 (gAI assistance vs no gAI assistance) x 2 (high vs low motivation) between subjects experimental design.

Additionally, a control condition with no gAI offloading and an alternative stage 1 task (to prevent the participants from building relational knowledge before they perform stage 2 and stage 3) will be employed in order to test hypothesis 1c: within the group with low motivation and no gAI, the analysis will include a two group (no gAI vs control condition) between subjects experimental design.

In order to test Hypothesis 6, a two-group between subjects design (high motivation vs low motivation) will be employed within the gAI condition.
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to each experimental group using block randomisation. When two participants are completing the task at the same time, they will be assigned to the same condition to ensure they receive uniform instructions and are not made aware of the details of other experimental conditions.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: We will recruit participants from the student population at Adam Mickiewicz University, Poznań (Poland), as well as the local population, through advertisements on campus and on social media. Participants must be at least 18 years old and native speakers of Polish. Participants will receive a 70PLN voucher after completing the experiment (50pln as advertised and 20pln as an additional bonus).
table.sample_size:
Our target sample size is 180 participants who complete the study. We will recruit up to 200 participants to account for those who withdraw or are excluded from the study. All participants meeting eligibility criteria will be included in the final analysis, up to a maximum of 200.
Data from participants who complete all 3 stages of the study (as well as working memory assessment and final questionnaire) will be included as long as participants follow the instructions and make genuine effort when completing the study. Specifically, we will exclude data from participants who fail to meet the following inclusion criteria:
- Respond correctly to at least 2 out of 3 control questions in stage 2, designed specifically to test attention to the material (where the answer can be found easily within one statement and does not require complex reasoning). These questions will be presented at the end and not included in the final score of the included participants.
- Not provide the same response to all questions within one stage
table.sample_size_rationale:
We used the software program G*Power to conduct a power analysis. Our goal was to obtain .85 power to detect a medium effect size of .25 at the standard .05 alpha error probability. 
The sample size is selected to ensure at least 36 participants per condition.
table.manipulated_variables:
Offloading will be manipulated by assigning participants to the gAI assistance condition or no gAI assistance condition in stage 1 of the study (access to chatGPT to support solving the questions).
- Motivation will be manipulated by adding additional incentives for half of the participants in the gAI assistance and no gAI assistance experimental conditions:
- A promise of an additional bonus of 20PLN if they perform in the top 33% of participants
information about (fictional) international comparison of results with participants in other countries
- A promise of providing individual results after the task is completed
The remaining participants will not receive any information about additional incentives. The information serves only to manipulate perceived importance of the task. During debriefing, all participants, regardless of condition, will receive an additional bonus and the opportunity to request individual results, and will be informed that there is no international comparison of results.
table.measured_variables:
Working memory capacity will be measured with shortened Symmetry Span and Operation Span tasks (e.g., Foster et al., 2015).

Reasoning performance and memory retention will be measured with a pseudoword network reasoning task created for the purpose of the experiment. This task includes 3 stages: 
Stage 1, the chunked reasoning task, consists of 18 questions about a network of pseudowords, which can be answered based on statements included in each question. All questions can be answered by choosing one answer from “yes/no/impossible to determine”.
Stage 2, the extended reasoning task, consists of 13 questions about the same pseudoword network, presented with 20 statements to support solving the questions. All questions can be answered by choosing one answer from “yes/no/impossible to determine”.
Stage 3, the memory retention task, includes 10 multiple choice questions (with one correct answer) about the same pseudoword network, which can be answered based on memory of network relations encoded in stages 1 and 2.
Accuracy of responses and time of completion at each stage will be used as separate dependent variables.

We will measure the number of requests to gAI in Stage 1.

To verify participants’ engagement, participants will provide their judgment regarding task difficulty on a scale of 1-7, and complete the Effort/Importance scale of the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (Deci et al., 1994).

Additionally, we will collect information regarding participants’ attitudes towards genAI (Juranek and Pochwatko, 2026) and frequency of use of genAI, as well as demographic information.
table.statistical_tests:
We will test each hypothesis with the following:
Hypothesis 1 a and 1b (Main effect of gAI assistance on accuracy) and Hypothesis 3 (Main effect of motivation on accuracy) will be tested in a 2 x 2 ANOVA, with stage 2 extended reasoning accuracy as a dependent variable.
 
Hypothesis 1c (Main effect of knowledge building on performance) will be tested in a t-test (no gAI experimental vs no gAI control) on accuracy of performance in stage 2 and memory performance in stage 3 (in low motivation group).
 
Hypothesis 2 (Main effect of gAI assistance on speed) and Hypothesis 4 (Main effect of motivation on speed) will be tested in a 2 x 2 ANOVA, with stage 2 completion time as a dependent variable.
 
Hypothesis 5 (Interaction of gAI assistance and motivation on memory performance) will be tested in a 2x2 ANOVA, with stage 3 memory performance as a dependent variable.
 
Hypothesis 6 (effect of motivation on the number of offloading requests) will be tested in a t-test (in gAI assistance group only).

 Hypothesis 7 (effect of working memory capacity on the number of offloading requests) will be tested in a linear regression (in gAI assistance group only).

table.title: The impact of cognitive support on the effectiveness of solving tasks
table.research_questions:
We will test the following hypotheses:

Hypothesis 1a (Offloading Advantage):
Participants with access to gAI assistance during the chunked reasoning task (stage 1) will perform better (higher accuracy) in the subsequent extended reasoning task (stage 2) than those without assistance.

Hypothesis 1b (Relational Knowledge Advantage):
Participants without gAI assistance during the chunked reasoning phase (stage 1) will perform better (higher accuracy) in the extended reasoning task (stage 2) than those with assistance.

Hypothesis 1c (Knowledge building vs Cognitive fatigue):
Participants in the control condition (without gAI assistance and with an alternative pseudoword chunked reasoning task in stage 1) will perform worse on the extended reasoning task (stage 2) and on the memory task (stage 3), compared to no gAI assistance experimental group which experiences a similar level of cognitive fatigue.

Hypothesis 2a (Speed via Offloading):
Participants with gAI assistance during the chunked reasoning phase (stage 1) will complete the extended reasoning task (stage 2) faster than those without assistance.

Hypothesis 2b (Speed via Internalization):
Participants without gAI assistance during the chunked reasoning phase (stage 1) will complete the extended reasoning task (stage 2) faster than those with assistance.

Hypothesis 3 (Motivation Advantage on accuracy)
We predict a main effect of motivation on performance in stage 2, whereby participants in the high motivation condition (with additional incentives) will demonstrate better accuracy. We will also examine an interaction between motivation and gAI assistance (see H1) on an exploratory basis.

Hypothesis 4 (Motivation Advantage on speed)
We predict a main effect of motivation on performance in stage 2, whereby speed of completion will be different for participants in the high motivation condition and low motivation condition. We will also examine an interaction between motivation and gAI assistance (see H2) on an exploratory basis.

Hypothesis 5 (Memory Internalization Advantage):
We predict a main effect of gAI assistance on memory performance in stage 3, whereby memory will be enhanced for participants without gAI assistance, as well as a main effect of motivation on memory performance in stage 3, whereby participants in the high motivation condition will demonstrate better memory for the pseudoword network. We will also examine an interaction between the two on an exploratory basis.

Hypothesis 6 (Cognitive Offloading Behaviour):
Within the gAI assistance condition, participants in the low motivation condition (no additional incentives) will engage in more cognitive offloading (i.e., more gAI requests) than those in the high motivation condition.

Hypothesis 7 (Offloading Modulated by Working Memory Capacity):
Participants in gAI assistance condition with lower working memory capacity will make more use of gAI assistance (i.e. more gAI requests) than those with higher working memory capacity.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview:
The study will include a 2 (gAI assistance vs no gAI assistance) x 2 (high vs low motivation) between subjects experimental design.

Additionally, a control condition with no gAI offloading and an alternative stage 1 task (to prevent the participants from building relational knowledge before they perform stage 2 and stage 3) will be employed in order to test hypothesis 1c: within the group with low motivation and no gAI, the analysis will include a two group (no gAI vs control condition) between subjects experimental design.

In order to test Hypothesis 6, a two-group between subjects design (high motivation vs low motivation) will be employed within the gAI condition.
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to each experimental group using block randomisation. When two participants are completing the task at the same time, they will be assigned to the same condition to ensure they receive uniform instructions and are not made aware of the details of other experimental conditions.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: We will recruit participants from the student population at Adam Mickiewicz University, Poznań (Poland), as well as the local population, through advertisements on campus and on social media. Participants must be at least 18 years old and native speakers of Polish. Participants will receive a 70PLN voucher after completing the experiment (50pln as advertised and 20pln as an additional bonus).
table.sample_size:
Our target sample size is 180 participants who complete the study. We will recruit up to 200 participants to account for those who withdraw or are excluded from the study. All participants meeting eligibility criteria will be included in the final analysis, up to a maximum of 200.
Data from participants who complete all 3 stages of the study (as well as working memory assessment and final questionnaire) will be included as long as participants follow the instructions and make genuine effort when completing the study. Specifically, we will exclude data from participants who fail to meet the following inclusion criteria:
- Respond correctly to at least 2 out of 3 control questions in stage 2, designed specifically to test attention to the material (where the answer can be found easily within one statement and does not require complex reasoning). These questions will be presented at the end and not included in the final score of the included participants.
- Not provide the same response to all questions within one stage
table.sample_size_rationale:
We used the software program G*Power to conduct a power analysis. Our goal was to obtain .85 power to detect a medium effect size of .25 at the standard .05 alpha error probability. 
The sample size is selected to ensure at least 36 participants per condition.
table.manipulated_variables:
Offloading will be manipulated by assigning participants to the gAI assistance condition or no gAI assistance condition in stage 1 of the study (access to chatGPT to support solving the questions).
- Motivation will be manipulated by adding additional incentives for half of the participants in the gAI assistance and no gAI assistance experimental conditions:
- A promise of an additional bonus of 20PLN if they perform in the top 33% of participants
information about (fictional) international comparison of results with participants in other countries
- A promise of providing individual results after the task is completed
The remaining participants will not receive any information about additional incentives. The information serves only to manipulate perceived importance of the task. During debriefing, all participants, regardless of condition, will receive an additional bonus and the opportunity to request individual results, and will be informed that there is no international comparison of results.
table.measured_variables:
Working memory capacity will be measured with shortened Symmetry Span and Operation Span tasks (e.g., Foster et al., 2015).

Reasoning performance and memory retention will be measured with a pseudoword network reasoning task created for the purpose of the experiment. This task includes 3 stages: 
Stage 1, the chunked reasoning task, consists of 18 questions about a network of pseudowords, which can be answered based on statements included in each question. All questions can be answered by choosing one answer from “yes/no/impossible to determine”.
Stage 2, the extended reasoning task, consists of 13 questions about the same pseudoword network, presented with 20 statements to support solving the questions. All questions can be answered by choosing one answer from “yes/no/impossible to determine”.
Stage 3, the memory retention task, includes 10 multiple choice questions (with one correct answer) about the same pseudoword network, which can be answered based on memory of network relations encoded in stages 1 and 2.
Accuracy of responses and time of completion at each stage will be used as separate dependent variables.

We will measure the number of requests to gAI in Stage 1.

To verify participants’ engagement, participants will provide their judgment regarding task difficulty on a scale of 1-7, and complete the Effort/Importance scale of the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (Deci et al., 1994).

Additionally, we will collect information regarding participants’ attitudes towards genAI (Juranek and Pochwatko, 2026) and frequency of use of genAI, as well as demographic information.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 102 columns across 5 data files.
#### Issues Identified
2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study procedure was approved by the institutional ethics committee (Opinion No.
live_data_statements: During the first stage, participants completed the task either with or without access to ChatGPT, while performance incentives were independently manipulated.

Participants assigned to 1 Preregistration: https://osf.io/59qtm/overview?view_only=ceab1b18a6254009b088ec1cab5a65fe; Supplementary materials: https://osf.io/sx2gv/overview?view_only=5c9af1952816462382f7cad344f7455c.
An additional control condition was included in which participants completed an alternative first-stage task without genAI assistance or motivational incentives.
Participants were randomly assigned to the experimental conditions using block randomisation.
Participants were recruited through printed posters, mailing lists, and paid advertisements on Facebook and Instagram targeting adult residents of the city in which the laboratory was located.
An additional four participants were excluded according to pre-registered criteria, because they failed to answer at least two of the three attention-check questions correctly.
These questions were designed to assess whether participants had attended to the presented material.
The final sample consisted of 193 participants: 128 women, 61 men, and four participants who did not specify their gender.
Consequently, participants had to construct and retain a structured representation of the network and derive conclusions that were not stated explicitly in the presented descriptions.
In the first stage, participants were presented with subsets of statements describing relatively small sections of the network.
This procedure was consistent with cognitive load theory, as it reduced the number of interacting elements that participants had to process simultaneously.
In the second stage, participants completed a more comprehensive reasoning task involving a substantially larger portion of the network.
Participants had access to additional paper-based materials with 20 information points, each containing one or two statements.
In the third stage, participants completed a 10-item memory test assessing their retention of information presented in both Stage 1 and Stage 2.
In SymSpan, participants had to remember locations of red squares in a 4 × 4 grid of potential locations.
After each item, a distractor task was presented, where participants were asked to judge symmetry of a displayed shape along its vertical axis.
In OSpan, participants had to remember a series of letters presented one at a time, with the letters randomly selected for each trial.
After each letter, participants had to solve a simple maths problem as a distractor task.
At the end of the block participants were asked to recall the letters in the correct order.
Additionally, participants provided information about the frequency of use of genAI tools and the type of tools they use.
Participants were tested in a computer laboratory, with up to two participants taking part simultaneously at separate workstations.
Upon arrival, participants were asked to switch off their mobile phones or activate airplane mode.
They then received information about the study, provided written informed consent, and were assigned a pseudonymised participant code.
Before the reasoning task, participants assigned to the incentive condition received standardised information intended to increase the perceived importance of their performance.
In the genAIassistance condition, ChatGPT was available on a separate monitor and participants were informed that they could use it freely to support their performance on the task.

Participants assigned to the control group showed numerically lower Stage 2 accuracy (𝑀 = 57.3%, 𝑆𝐷 = 17.9%) than participants in the comparable experimental condition with no genAI access and no incentives (𝑀 = 64.1%, 𝑆𝐷 = 15.2%).

Further, the effect of incentives was significant among participants without genAI access, such that participants completed the task more slowly when additional incentives were provided (EMM = 54.30; 95%CI[44.03; 66.28]) than when no additional incentives were provided (EMM = 39.00; 95%CI [31.04; 48.40]; estimate = -0.216, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.060, 𝑡(153) = -3.584, 𝑝 < .001).
Because the last category was both small and heterogeneous, these three participants were excluded from subsequent comparisons between patterns of ChatGPT use.
After initially working with or without genAI support, participants were required to reason independently about relations distributed across the same broader knowledge network.
Thus, genAI facilitated performance on the immediate task, whereas incentives primarily increased the amount of time participants were willing to invest.
In Stage 1, participants had to identify relevant information and integrate relations across multiple statements.
The item-level analysis also showed that participants were more likely to turn to genAI when they encountered more difficult questions.
Interestingly, although working memory capacity did not predict overall genAI use across participants, question difficulty predicted when participants were more likely to seek assistance.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, `source()` call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

```{r}

), "Runs after" = c("—", "—"), Basis = c("none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, 
-2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 2 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) is increasingly used to support learning and problem solving, but it remains unclear how relying on such support affects people's ability to reason independently afterwards.
We investigated whether using genAI to solve a complex reasoning task influences subsequent reasoning, memory, and effort when the technology is no longer available.

In a preregistered laboratory experiment with a final sample of 193 participants, we used a three-stage relational reasoning task developed for the study, in which participants learned and reasoned about a network of fictional entities and their relationships.
During the first stage, participants completed the task either with or without access to ChatGPT, while performance incentives were independently manipulated.
All participants then completed a more complex reasoning task based on the same relational network without genAI support, followed by a memory test.
GenAI support improved accuracy during the initial task and reduced perceived difficulty.
In the subsequent unaided reasoning task, prior genAI use was associated with some evidence of poorer independent reasoning.
GenAI use was also associated with weaker adjustment of effort to incentives and task difficulty once the tool was removed.
No clear effects were observed on later memory.

Overall, the findings highlight the importance of distinguishing successful AI-assisted task completion from the knowledge construction and effort regulation needed to apply the same information independently.
Digital technologies increasingly shape how people learn, acquire knowledge, and solve problems.
When engaging in these activities, humans frequently reduce cognitive demands by offloading cognitive processes to the environment (Clark & Chalmers, 1998; Risko & Gilbert, 2016).
text.formatted: When engaging in these activities, humans frequently reduce cognitive demands by offloading cognitive processes to the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Clark & Chalmers, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Risko & Gilbert, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Traditionally, external tools such as written notes, calculators, and digital devices have supported relatively simple cognitive operations.

Recent advances in generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) offer unprecedented potential to delegate higher-level cognitive functions traditionally associated with humans, such as decision-making, creativity, and reasoning (Chlebowski, Ratajczyk, & Wyrwa, 2026; Makridakis, 2017; Noy & Zhang, 2023).
text.formatted: Recent advances in generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) offer unprecedented potential to delegate higher-level cognitive functions traditionally associated with humans, such as decision-making, creativity, and reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chlebowski, Ratajczyk, & Wyrwa, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Makridakis, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Noy & Zhang, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Although cognitive offloading can improve performance by reducing cognitive demands, it may also reduce the internal processing required for learning and knowledge construction (Skulmowski, 2023).
Offloading higher-order processes to genAI may therefore have consequences for knowledge acquisition subsequent independent reasoning and the regulation of effort on related tasks.

Cognitive load theory (CLT) describes how the information processing load induced by learning tasks affects the ability to process new information and construct knowledge in long-term memory (Sweller, 2011).
text.formatted: Cognitive load theory (CLT) describes how the information processing load induced by learning tasks affects the ability to process new information and construct knowledge in long-term memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Sweller, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: A central concept in CLT is element interactivity, referring to the number of interacting elements that must be processed simultaneously in working memory.
Organising information into schemas in long-term memory reduces effective element interactivity and the demands placed on working memory.

For example, when faced with high element interactivity tasks, learners may resort to rote learning, thereby avoiding the additional information processing but failing to create meaningful understanding, i.e., failing to create organised information schemas in long-term memory.
Cognitive offloading provides another way of reducing processing demands by transferring some cognitive operations to external resources (see Pea, 1985).
text.formatted: Cognitive offloading provides another way of reducing processing demands by transferring some cognitive operations to external resources (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Pea, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: While this can free internal resources and facilitate immediate performance, offloading operations involved in organising and integrating information may also reduce the processing through which knowledge is constructed.

Consistent with this possibility, cognitive offloading has been associated with memory decay (Kelly & Risko, 2019), reduced effort (Risko, Huh, McLean, & Ferguson, 2017), altered memory strategies (Scarampi & Gilbert, 2020), and decreased acquisition of procedural knowledge (Moritz, Meyerhoff, & Schwan, 2020).
text.formatted: Consistent with this possibility, cognitive offloading has been associated with memory decay <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Kelly & Risko, 2019)</ref>, reduced effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Risko, Huh, McLean, & Ferguson, 2017)</ref>, altered memory strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Scarampi & Gilbert, 2020)</ref>, and decreased acquisition of procedural knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Moritz, Meyerhoff, & Schwan, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Technologies like GPS, for instance, have been shown to impair spatial memory in both short and long terms (Dahmani & Bohbot, 2020; Fenech, Drews, & Bakdash, 2010), which may stem from the reduced engagement with the problem's deeper structures (O'Hara & Payne, 1998) and the divided attention during use (Gardony, Brunyé, & Taylor, 2015).
text.formatted: Technologies like GPS, for instance, have been shown to impair spatial memory in both short and long terms <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dahmani & Bohbot, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Fenech, Drews, & Bakdash, 2010)</ref>, which may stem from the reduced engagement with the problem's deeper structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(O'Hara & Payne, 1998)</ref> and the divided attention during use <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Gardony, Brunyé, & Taylor, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Decisions about whether and how much to offload depend on metacognitive evaluations of task demands and available cognitive resources. Skulmowski (2023) proposed a cognitive model of digital externalisation based on CLT, according to which lower working-memory capacity or perceived cognitive capacity and higher cognitive load increase offloading, whereas higher perceived value of information decreases it.
text.formatted: Decisions about whether and how much to offload depend on metacognitive evaluations of task demands and available cognitive resources. <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Skulmowski (2023)</ref> proposed a cognitive model of digital externalisation based on CLT, according to which lower working-memory capacity or perceived cognitive capacity and higher cognitive load increase offloading, whereas higher perceived value of information decreases it.

text.text: Thus, reliance on external resources depends not only on task demands but also on individuals' assessment of their own cognitive resources.
GenAI systems can generate and transform text, images, code, and other content.
Many text-based applications rely on large language models trained to predict linguistic sequences and subsequently fine-tuned using human preference data (Cao et al., 2023; Demszky et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Many text-based applications rely on large language models trained to predict linguistic sequences and subsequently fine-tuned using human preference data <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cao et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Demszky et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Their ability to summarise, compare, transform, and integrate information allows users to offload not only routine operations but also higher-order processes central to reasoning (Baidoo-Anu & Ansah, 2023; Orrù, Piarulli, Conversano, & Gemignani, 2023) This ability makes them a popular tool among learners, who may offload learning-related tasks regardless of the consequences for the learning process.
text.formatted: Their ability to summarise, compare, transform, and integrate information allows users to offload not only routine operations but also higher-order processes central to reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baidoo-Anu & Ansah, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Orrù, Piarulli, Conversano, & Gemignani, 2023)</ref> This ability makes them a popular tool among learners, who may offload learning-related tasks regardless of the consequences for the learning process.

text.text: Although offloading may free up cognitive resources, it may also replace processing that is necessary for learning, metacognitive evaluation, and subsequent independent reasoning.
Evidence from empirical studies presents a similarly complex picture.
Several findings document clear benefits.

AI-based writing tools have been shown to improve output quality for students learning English as a foreign language (Marzuki, Widiati, Rusdin, Darwin, & Indrawati, 2023), while structured uses of genAI, including language-learning chatbots, automated feedback, and personalised recommendations, have been associated with gains in learning performance and higher-order thinking skills (Wang, Cheung, Neitzel, & Chai, 2025).
text.formatted: AI-based writing tools have been shown to improve output quality for students learning English as a foreign language <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Marzuki, Widiati, Rusdin, Darwin, & Indrawati, 2023)</ref>, while structured uses of genAI, including language-learning chatbots, automated feedback, and personalised recommendations, have been associated with gains in learning performance and higher-order thinking skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Wang, Cheung, Neitzel, & Chai, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Related studies suggest that active engagement with genAI, particularly when students use it to explore ideas rather than outsource the task, can support knowledge acquisition and application (Jo, 2024), as well as creative, critical, and reflective thinking (Essel, Vlachopoulos, Essuman, & Amankwa, 2024).
text.formatted: Related studies suggest that active engagement with genAI, particularly when students use it to explore ideas rather than outsource the task, can support knowledge acquisition and application <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Jo, 2024)</ref>, as well as creative, critical, and reflective thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Essel, Vlachopoulos, Essuman, & Amankwa, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Benefits have also been demonstrated outside education.
For example, Noy and Zhang (2023) found that professionals completing writing tasks with ChatGPT produced higher quality outputs and completed their tasks more quickly.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Noy and Zhang (2023)</ref> found that professionals completing writing tasks with ChatGPT produced higher quality outputs and completed their tasks more quickly.

text.text: There are also documented risks.

Excessive reliance on genAI has been linked to poorer learning outcomes, memory difficulties, and declines in creativity and problem-solving performance (Abbas, Jam, & Khan, 2024). Fulbright and Morrison (2024), for example, found that although average performance was comparable between participants using ChatGPT and a control group, a subset of ChatGPT users showed poorer problem-solving performance, potentially because the tool directed attention towards irrelevant information.
text.formatted: Excessive reliance on genAI has been linked to poorer learning outcomes, memory difficulties, and declines in creativity and problem-solving performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abbas, Jam, & Khan, 2024)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Fulbright and Morrison (2024)</ref>, for example, found that although average performance was comparable between participants using ChatGPT and a control group, a subset of ChatGPT users showed poorer problem-solving performance, potentially because the tool directed attention towards irrelevant information.

text.text: The use of genAI may also affect the accuracy of metacognitive judgments about one's own performance and capabilities (Urban et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The use of genAI may also affect the accuracy of metacognitive judgments about one's own performance and capabilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Urban et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A closely related concept is metacognitive laziness, introduced by Fan et al. (2025) to describe a pattern in which learners become overly reliant on genAI, shifting both task execution and aspects of cognitive and metacognitive regulation to the tool.
text.formatted: A closely related concept is metacognitive laziness, introduced by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Fan et al. (2025)</ref> to describe a pattern in which learners become overly reliant on genAI, shifting both task execution and aspects of cognitive and metacognitive regulation to the tool.

text.text: In their study, Chat-GPT support improved short-term essay performance, but no significant gains were found for knowledge acquisition or transfer.
The authors suggest that this pattern may reflect reduced involvement in self-regulatory processes such as monitoring, evaluation, and deeper reflection.

A similar pattern emerges from neuroimaging research. Kosmyna et al. (2025) reported weaker neural engagement and poorer recall in participants who wrote essays with genAI support compared with those who used search engines or worked without external assistance.
text.formatted: A similar pattern emerges from neuroimaging research. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Kosmyna et al. (2025)</ref> reported weaker neural engagement and poorer recall in participants who wrote essays with genAI support compared with those who used search engines or worked without external assistance.

text.text: Participants in the genAI-assisted condition also showed lower cognitive engagement, frequently relying on copy-and-paste behaviour when incorporating AI-generated content.
Reduced neural engagement persisted when participants who had previously used genAI later completed the task independently.

Another concern is the potential homogenising effect of LLMs on expression and thought. Sourati, Ziabari, and Dehghani (2026) argue that LLMs may standardise not only language but also perspectives and reasoning strategies because their outputs tend to privilege dominant, frequent, and easily generalisable patterns.
text.formatted: Another concern is the potential homogenising effect of LLMs on expression and thought. <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Sourati, Ziabari, and Dehghani (2026)</ref> argue that LLMs may standardise not only language but also perspectives and reasoning strategies because their outputs tend to privilege dominant, frequent, and easily generalisable patterns.

text.text: Thus, habitual reliance on genAI may reduce engagement in one's own reasoning and narrow the range of linguistic, perspectival, and inferential possibilities that users consider.
The effects of genAI appear to depend on the context and manner of its use.

Evidence suggests that benefits tend to emerge when genAI is used for feedback, conceptual scaffolding, guiding reflection, and individualised support, whereas harms are more likely when genAI begins to replace cognitive work that is central to a given task, such as writing, reasoning, or problem solving (Cabitza & Vicente, 2026; Lo, Hew, & Jong, 2024).
text.formatted: Evidence suggests that benefits tend to emerge when genAI is used for feedback, conceptual scaffolding, guiding reflection, and individualised support, whereas harms are more likely when genAI begins to replace cognitive work that is central to a given task, such as writing, reasoning, or problem solving <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cabitza & Vicente, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Lo, Hew, & Jong, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Whether genAI supports or replaces task-relevant cognitive processing may be particularly important for relational reasoning, which is central to human learning Dumas, Alexander, and Grossnickle (2013).
text.formatted: Whether genAI supports or replaces task-relevant cognitive processing may be particularly important for relational reasoning, which is central to human learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Dumas, Alexander, and Grossnickle (2013)</ref>.

text.text: Reasoning involves integrating internally stored knowledge with newly available information to construct a coherent representation of the problem.
Acquiring the representation allows its use to make new inferences in the future (Stenning & Van Lambalgen, 2012).
text.formatted: Acquiring the representation allows its use to make new inferences in the future <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Stenning & Van Lambalgen, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Here, offloading to genAI poses the greatest risk if it disrupts the formation of the representation.

For example, learning that a given organism has a particular characteristic (e.g., that amphibians breathe partly through their skin) requires relating that fact to habitat, physiology, and comparison with other classes of animals.
Having genAI generate these links can bypass the very processing through which the knowledge is encoded.
Relational knowledge supports reasoning by preserving the structural organisation of information and allowing relations to be applied in novel situations (Halford, Wilson, & Phillips, 2010).
text.formatted: Relational knowledge supports reasoning by preserving the structural organisation of information and allowing relations to be applied in novel situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Halford, Wilson, & Phillips, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: According to CLT, constructing such representations becomes difficult when the number of interacting elements exceeds available working-memory resources; organising these elements into schemas in long-term memory reduces their effective complexity and supports subsequent processing (Sweller, 2011).
text.formatted: According to CLT, constructing such representations becomes difficult when the number of interacting elements exceeds available working-memory resources; organising these elements into schemas in long-term memory reduces their effective complexity and supports subsequent processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Sweller, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: GenAI can reduce these demands by organising and integrating information, but may also allow users to obtain correct answers without constructing the underlying schemas themselves.
Consequently, immediate performance may improve at the cost of the relational knowledge required for later independent reasoning.
External access to information may not fully substitute for internally represented relational knowledge.

Moreover, when people do not expect information to be useful later, they may be more willing to offload it, potentially impairing memory and increasing future reliance on external sources (Storm, Stone, & Benjamin, 2017).
text.formatted: Moreover, when people do not expect information to be useful later, they may be more willing to offload it, potentially impairing memory and increasing future reliance on external sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Storm, Stone, & Benjamin, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This issue is particularly relevant to genAI and its place in education and the learning process, because it can externalise not only access to individual pieces of information, but also the integration and transformation of those pieces into a coherent relational representation.
Successful learning outcomes are influenced by motivation, which is linked to task engagement and persistence (Howard, Bureau, Guay, Chong, & Ryan, 2021; Reeve & Lee, 2014).
text.formatted: Successful learning outcomes are influenced by motivation, which is linked to task engagement and persistence <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Howard, Bureau, Guay, Chong, & Ryan, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Reeve & Lee, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Research applying cognitive load theory to task engagement suggests that high cognitive load leads to reduced perception of self-efficacy and hurts motivation (Bandura, 1982; Feldon, Franco, Chao, Peugh, & Maahs-Fladung, 2018), while load reduction leads to higher motivation and higher engagement with the task, along with better outcomes (e.g., Evans, Vansteenkiste, Parker, Kingsford-Smith, & Zhou, 2024; Noy & Zhang, 2023; Skulmowski, Pradel, Kühnert, Brunnett, & Rey, 2016; Wu, Liu, Ruan, Chen, & Xie, 2025).
text.formatted: Research applying cognitive load theory to task engagement suggests that high cognitive load leads to reduced perception of self-efficacy and hurts motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bandura, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Feldon, Franco, Chao, Peugh, & Maahs-Fladung, 2018)</ref>, while load reduction leads to higher motivation and higher engagement with the task, along with better outcomes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Evans, Vansteenkiste, Parker, Kingsford-Smith, & Zhou, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Noy & Zhang, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Skulmowski, Pradel, Kühnert, Brunnett, & Rey, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Wu, Liu, Ruan, Chen, & Xie, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In line with these observations, reducing cognitive load by offloading the task to genAI should lead participants to experience increased self-efficacy beliefs and greater motivation to perform well on the task, suggesting yet another benefit of genAI tools for enhanced performance.
However, theories of motivation paint a more complex picture.
The central factor in how much effort is exerted for task performance is task difficulty.

Motivation intensity theory (MIT; Brehm & Self, 1989; Brehm, Wright, Solomon, Silka, & Greenberg, 1983; Richter, Gendolla, & Wright, 2016) postulates that the amount of energy deployed for task completion is dependent on task demands and available resources.
text.formatted: Motivation intensity theory (MIT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Brehm & Self, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Brehm, Wright, Solomon, Silka, & Greenberg, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Richter, Gendolla, & Wright, 2016)</ref> postulates that the amount of energy deployed for task completion is dependent on task demands and available resources.

text.text: Challenging tasks "energise" individuals and present higher goal attractiveness, which leads to greater effort.

Indeed, higher task difficulty increases the amount of biological and mental resources needed, as evidenced by increased heart rate or blood pressure in preparation for a difficult task (Richter et al., 2016; Wright, Shaw, & Jones, 1990).
text.formatted: Indeed, higher task difficulty increases the amount of biological and mental resources needed, as evidenced by increased heart rate or blood pressure in preparation for a difficult task <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Richter et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Wright, Shaw, & Jones, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: However, at a very high level of difficulty, when the task starts to seem impossible to perform, the amount of required resources is not proportionate to the task requirements, and therefore people report lower intended effort and lower motivation to engage in the task (Brehm et al., 1983; Silvestrini, Musslick, Berry, & Vassena, 2023).
text.formatted: However, at a very high level of difficulty, when the task starts to seem impossible to perform, the amount of required resources is not proportionate to the task requirements, and therefore people report lower intended effort and lower motivation to engage in the task <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brehm et al., 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Silvestrini, Musslick, Berry, & Vassena, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: MIT's account of perceived difficulty relates to the task's objective demands, as well as one's perceived ability to meet those demands, such that lower confidence in one's own capability increases the effort perceived as necessary for a given task (Brehm & Self, 1989; Wright, 1996).
text.formatted: MIT's account of perceived difficulty relates to the task's objective demands, as well as one's perceived ability to meet those demands, such that lower confidence in one's own capability increases the effort perceived as necessary for a given task <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Brehm & Self, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Wright, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: This perspective is related to the expected value of control (EVC) theory, which states that individuals decide how much effort to allocate to a task by weighing the potential benefits of allocating control against associated costs (Shenhav, Botvinick, & Cohen, 2013; Silvestrini et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This perspective is related to the expected value of control (EVC) theory, which states that individuals decide how much effort to allocate to a task by weighing the potential benefits of allocating control against associated costs <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Shenhav, Botvinick, & Cohen, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Silvestrini et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: When the cost is deemed too high relative to the amount of control required by the task, energy is conserved by allocating less effort to it.

Additionally, a promise of a reward leads to increased performance on cognitive control trials (Padmala & Pessoa, 2011; Umemoto & Holroyd, 2015) as a reward increases the attractiveness of the goal and therefore the amount of effort deployed to achieve it.
text.formatted: Additionally, a promise of a reward leads to increased performance on cognitive control trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Padmala & Pessoa, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Umemoto & Holroyd, 2015)</ref> as a reward increases the attractiveness of the goal and therefore the amount of effort deployed to achieve it.

text.text: Thus, providing people with additional incentives on top of a relatively challenging task should increase their motivation and the amount of effort exerted in the task.
These theories and their associated predictions lend themselves to address the question of offloading cognitive load to genAI and its implications for learning.

Offloading to genAI may reduce task difficulty, which would reduce the amount of effort participants mobilise in the task, compared to a group without access to genAI, as they employ the lowest amount of resources required to perform the task.
As per MIT, an incentive could counteract this effect by increasing the amount of effort mobilised.
On the other hand, offloading may also disrupt construction of knowledge required for subsequent reasoning, which makes it appear more difficult.

As participants' estimate of their own capabilities will be reduced or uncertain, perceived difficulty may increase, which increases the amount of effort mobilised, compared to a group without access to genAI.

Current research on genAI use and effort has not disentangled these predictions. Huffstadt (2026) found that participants who used genAI at work reported reduced mental effort, which in turn predicted increased effort, but other studies report the opposite pattern of results.
text.formatted: Current research on genAI use and effort has not disentangled these predictions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Huffstadt (2026)</ref> found that participants who used genAI at work reported reduced mental effort, which in turn predicted increased effort, but other studies report the opposite pattern of results.

text.text: Dell'Acqua (2022) suggested that high-performing genAI may incentivise humans to decrease effort.
He found that HR professionals who were given high quality genAI assistance produced poorer resume evaluations than those who were given low quality assistance.

It is possible that the mistaken (or inflated) perception of fluency and competence in human-genAI interaction negatively influenced participants' engagement with the task and the amount of resources they mobilised, in line with motivation theories.

Relatedly, Liu, Christian, Dumbalska, Bakker, and Dubey (2026) found that participants who performed maths tasks with genAI were later less likely to complete more maths questions independently, which the authors attributed to reduced persistence.
text.formatted: Relatedly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Liu, Christian, Dumbalska, Bakker, and Dubey (2026)</ref> found that participants who performed maths tasks with genAI were later less likely to complete more maths questions independently, which the authors attributed to reduced persistence.

text.text: They proposed that after working with genAI, participants' estimate regarding how much time and effort a task should take, is calibrated to genAI-assisted performance and a subsequent task appears to require much more effort and resources, due to a metacognitive decay.
This interpretation is in line with theories of motivation, where feeling out of one's depth regarding task difficulty reduces motivation.
This effect was not found for participants who were solving maths tasks independently throughout the experiment.
Similarly, Wu et al. (2025) examined participants' motivation both after performing a genAI assisted task (or an unassisted control task) and a subsequent independently performed task.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Wu et al. (2025)</ref> examined participants' motivation both after performing a genAI assisted task (or an unassisted control task) and a subsequent independently performed task.

text.text: They found evidence for increased motivation for the genAI assisted task, compared to a control group who worked independently, but subsequently those who were asked to stop working with genAI reported a larger drop in motivation than those who were working independently throughout the experiment.
It appears that genAI tools cause people to overestimate later (independent) task difficulty and perceive it as too difficult to be worth engaging their resources (as per MIT).
However, neither study directly tested how genAI affects motivation when subsequent performance depends on knowledge constructed during the assisted task.
In Wu et al. (2025), the successive tasks were unrelated, whereas in Liu et al. (2026), the subsequent task did not depend on knowledge acquired during the genAI-assisted phase.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Wu et al. (2025)</ref>, the successive tasks were unrelated, whereas in <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Liu et al. (2026)</ref>, the subsequent task did not depend on knowledge acquired during the genAI-assisted phase.

text.text: Moreover, participants in the latter study knew in advance that genAI support would later be removed.
To our knowledge, no study has orthogonally manipulated genAI access and motivational incentives, leaving their joint effects on knowledge construction and effort regulation unclear.

To examine how cognitive offloading to genAI and performance incentives shape subsequent independent reasoning, effort regulation, and knowledge retention, we conducted a three-stage experiment based on a complex relational reasoning task.
The study comprised an initial reasoning task (Stage 1), a subsequent independent reasoning task (Stage 2), and a memory test (Stage 3).
GenAI access and performance incentives were independently manipulated, with genAI available only during Stage 1.
An additional control condition completed a structurally similar but unrelated Stage 1 task without genAI, followed by the same Stage 2 and Stage 3 tasks as the experimental groups.

Based on the theoretical considerations outlined above, we formulated three sets of hypotheses concerning the consequences of genAI assistance, the effects of performance incentives, and the determinants of cognitive offloading behaviour.
The hypotheses specified below were preregistered.
The first set of hypotheses concerns two competing consequences of cognitive offloading to genAI for subsequent performance.

On the one hand, by reducing the cognitive demands of the initial task, genAI assistance may limit the accumulation of cognitive fatigue, leaving more resources available for subsequent independent reasoning.

This prediction is consistent with findings from sequentialtask paradigms showing that sustained effortful cognitive control can impair performance on a subsequent demanding task (Hagger, Wood, Stiff, & Chatzisarantis, 2010), as well as research showing that cognitive offloading can benefit performance on concurrent or subsequent cognitively demanding tasks (Runge, Frings, & Tempel, 2019; Storm & Stone, 2015).
text.formatted: This prediction is consistent with findings from sequentialtask paradigms showing that sustained effortful cognitive control can impair performance on a subsequent demanding task <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hagger, Wood, Stiff, & Chatzisarantis, 2010)</ref>, as well as research showing that cognitive offloading can benefit performance on concurrent or subsequent cognitively demanding tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Runge, Frings, & Tempel, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Storm & Stone, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, participants who use genAI during Stage 1 may perform better and more efficiently in Stage 2.

On the other hand, offloading the integration of information to genAI may reduce engagement with the underlying relational structure, resulting in weaker internal representations and consequently poorer subsequent reasoning and memory.

The control condition allows these accounts to be distinguished by comparing participants who completed a similarly demanding Stage 1 task, and should therefore experience comparable cognitive fatigue, but who did not acquire relational knowledge relevant to the subsequent stages.

H1a: Participants with access to genAI assistance during the chunked reasoning task (Stage 1) will achieve higher accuracy in the subsequent network-level reasoning task (Stage 2) than those without assistance.

H1b: Participants without genAI assistance during the chunked reasoning phase (Stage 1) will achieve higher accuracy in the subsequent network-level reasoning task (Stage 2) than those with assistance.

H1c: Participants in the control condition, who complete an alternative chunked reasoning task in Stage 1, will show lower accuracy in the network-level reasoning task (Stage 2) and the memory task (Stage 3) than participants in the no-genAI-assistance experimental condition.
H2a: Participants with genAI assistance during the chunked reasoning phase (Stage 1) will complete the subsequent network-level reasoning task (Stage 2) faster than those without assistance.
H2b: Participants without genAI assistance during the chunked reasoning phase (Stage 1) will complete the subsequent network-level reasoning task (Stage 2) faster than those with assistance.
H3: Participants without genAI assistance during the chunked reasoning phase (Stage 1) will demonstrate better memory performance in Stage 3 than those with assistance.
Participants in the performance-incentive condition will also demonstrate better memory performance than those in the no-incentive condition.
The interaction between genAI assistance and performance incentives will be examined on an exploratory basis.
Performance incentives may influence task performance by changing how much effort individuals are willing to mobilise.
According to motivation intensity theory, effort investment depends not only on task demands but also on the importance and attractiveness of successful performance.
Incentives can increase the value of success and thereby justify greater investment of cognitive resources, particularly in demanding tasks.
Accordingly, participants receiving additional performance incentives may invest more effort in Stage 2, which may translate into higher accuracy and differences in completion time.
Because genAI assistance during Stage 1 may alter perceived task demands and subsequent effort regulation, we additionally examine whether the effects of incentives depend on prior access to genAI.
H4: Participants in the performance-incentive condition will achieve higher accuracy in Stage 2 than participants in the no-incentive condition.
We will also examine the interaction between performance incentives and prior genAI assistance on an exploratory basis.
H5: Completion time in Stage 2 will differ between participants in the performance-incentive and no-incentive conditions.
We will also examine the interaction between performance incentives and prior genAI assistance on an exploratory basis.
The extent to which individuals rely on external cognitive support is not uniform, but depends on both taskrelated and individual factors.

Cognitive offloading can be understood as a metacognitively regulated strategy in which individuals balance the cognitive costs of performing a task internally against the benefits of using an external resource.
Lower working memory capacity is expected to increase reliance on offloading, as fewer internal resources are available for maintaining and integrating task information.
In addition, performance incentives may reduce offloading by increasing the perceived importance of engaging with and retaining task-relevant information.
We therefore examine whether engaging in the use of genAI support is predicted by both performance incentives and individual working memory capacity.

H6: Within the genAI-assistance condition, participants in the no-incentive condition will engage in more cognitive offloading, operationalised as a greater number of genAI requests, than participants in the performance-incentive condition.

H7: Within the genAI-assistance condition, participants with lower working memory capacity will engage in more cognitive offloading, operationalised as a greater number of genAI requests than participants with higher working memory capacity.

The primary dependent variables were response accuracy in each of the three task stages and the time required to complete Stage 1 and Stage 2.

Additional dependent variables included subjective cognitive effort and perceived task difficulty.

Participants were randomly assigned to the experimental conditions using block randomisation.
The order of questions within each task was randomised for each participant.
Participants were recruited through printed posters, mailing lists, and paid advertisements on Facebook and Instagram targeting adult residents of the city in which the laboratory was located.
The advertisements invited individuals to participate in a scientific study on problem-solving and decision-making.
Eligibility criteria were being at least 18 years old, being a native speaker of Polish, and having no prior experience with the research team's previous studies on this topic.
Data were collected between 2 March and 22 May 2026.
Participants received vouchers worth 70 PLN (approximately 16 EUR) as compensation for their participation.
This amount comprised the advertised compensation of 50 PLN and an additional bonus of 20 PLN.
A total of 198 individuals participated in the study.
One participant was excluded from all analyses because of noncompliance with the experimental procedure.
An additional four participants were excluded according to pre-registered criteria, because they failed to answer at least two of the three attention-check questions correctly.
These questions were designed to assess whether participants had attended to the presented material.
The final sample consisted of 193 participants: 128 women, 61 men, and four participants who did not specify their gender.
Participants' mean age was 25.1 years (𝑆𝐷 = 7.0).

text.text: >Materials
text.formatted: <head n="2.3." >Materials</head>

text.text: The study employed a task specifically developed to assess the retention of relational knowledge and the ability to reason on the basis of that knowledge.
It comprised three consecutive stages: (1) a chunk-based reasoning task, (2) a network-level reasoning task, and (3) a memory-retention test.
The task was based on a complex network of pseudowords representing entities, their attributes, and the relationships among them.
In the main version of the task, the entities were fictitious biological or mythical creatures inhabiting different environments.
In the control condition, they were fictitious celestial bodies located in fictitious galaxies.

Participants encountered statements defining the entities and their relationships, such as "Kikara lives in the desert and is active only at night", "Bekierc is smaller than Kikara", and "Grzuniak is a type of Hosaluk."
3  The complete main network contained 15 entities and several dozen attributes and relationships.
It was described by 82 unique logical propositions, although individual sentences could encode more than one proposition.
The network was designed to be too complex to process in its entirety within working memory capacity.
Consequently, participants had to construct and retain a structured representation of the network and derive conclusions that were not stated explicitly in the presented descriptions.
The reasoning problems were enthymematic, sometimes requiring commonsense assumptions in addition to the explicitly presented information.
In the first stage, participants were presented with subsets of statements describing relatively small sections of the network.
Each subset was followed by questions that required participants to transform and integrate the available information rather than retrieve 3 The task was originally developed in Polish.
an explicitly stated answer.
Example questions included "Is Grzuniak bigger than Blusotnia?", "Does Puładra have more legs than Kikara?", and "Are the creatures mentioned above active at the same time of day?"
Figure 1 shows an example question.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> shows an example question.

text.text: The information was divided into chunks to limit cognitive load and facilitate the construction of a coherent mental representation of the network.
This procedure was consistent with cognitive load theory, as it reduced the number of interacting elements that participants had to process simultaneously.
The chunks varied in size and in the difficulty of the corresponding questions.
Each question was based on four to eight statements.
Participants selected one of three response options: yes, no, or impossible to determine.
In the second stage, participants completed a more comprehensive reasoning task involving a substantially larger portion of the network.
This stage assessed their ability to integrate and apply relational information encountered during the preceding stage.
Participants had access to additional paper-based materials with 20 information points, each containing one or two statements.
The order of these information points was randomised for each participant.
Together, they contained 48 logical propositions that had previously appeared in the chunk-based reasoning task.
Participants answered 13 questions requiring the integration of information distributed across the 20 information points, which contained all information necessary to answer the questions.
Example questions included "Is Blusotnia the largest creature living in the tropics?"
and "Are there any herbivorous creatures with antennae in the tropics?".
As in the first stage, the available response options were yes, no, and impossible to determine.
Three control questions were presented at the end.
These were simpler questions which could be answered based on a single proposition and were not included in the analysis.
In the third stage, participants completed a 10-item memory test assessing their retention of information presented in both Stage 1 and Stage 2.
Each question had four single-choice response options.
Example questions included "Which creature hunts Kołoląki?"
and "In which environment or environments do Mioczki live?"

Working memory capacity.

In addition to the reasoning tasks, we measured working memory capacity with shortened complex span task (Foster et al., 2015), which consisted of two blocks of Symmetry Span (SymSpan) and one block of Operation Span (OSpan) tasks.
text.formatted: In addition to the reasoning tasks, we measured working memory capacity with shortened complex span task <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Foster et al., 2015)</ref>, which consisted of two blocks of Symmetry Span (SymSpan) and one block of Operation Span (OSpan) tasks.

text.text: In SymSpan, participants had to remember locations of red squares in a 4 × 4 grid of potential locations.
After each item, a distractor task was presented, where participants were asked to judge symmetry of a displayed shape along its vertical axis.
Each block comprised four trials, with set sizes ranging from 2 to 5 locations.
Scores were calculated by summing the number of red square locations correctly recalled in the correct order.
In OSpan, participants had to remember a series of letters presented one at a time, with the letters randomly selected for each trial.
After each letter, participants had to solve a simple maths problem as a distractor task.
At the end of the block participants were asked to recall the letters in the correct order.
Scores were calculated by summing the number of letters correctly recalled in the correct position.
Working memory capacity was calculated as the average of the scores from OSpan and SymSpan tasks.
Task difficulty for each reasoning task (chunk-based reasoning, network reasoning and memory test) was self-reported by participants on a 7-point scale, from "very easy" to "very difficult".

In order to measure perceived importance of the task and how much effort participants put into solving the tasks, we used the Effort/Importance scale of the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (e.g., Deci, Eghrari, Patrick, and Leone (1994) ).

text.text: The scale was translated to Polish by the authors, with back translations verified by two highly proficient Polish-English bilinguals (including a professional translator).
Attitudes towards and use of genAI.
We also collected information regarding participants' attitudes towards genAI using the Polish adaptation of the AI attitude scale (AIAS-4; Grassini, 2023; Juranek & Pochwatko, 2026).
