text.text: Additionally, participants provided information about the frequency of use of genAI tools and the type of tools they use.

Based on the conversations with ChatGPT conducted by participants in the genAI condition during the chunked reasoning task, we calculated the number of messages per reasoning question sent to ChatGPT by each participant, as well as the number of unique reasoning questions each participant sent to Chat-GPT.
The data was used to analyse the relationship between genAI use frequency and style, and performance on both the chunk reasoning task and the network reasoning task.
The study procedure was approved by the institutional ethics committee (Opinion No.
Participants were tested in a computer laboratory, with up to two participants taking part simultaneously at separate workstations.
The workstations were arranged so that participants could not see each other's responses or interact during the tasks.
Upon arrival, participants were asked to switch off their mobile phones or activate airplane mode.
They then received information about the study, provided written informed consent, and were assigned a pseudonymised participant code.
The complete laboratory session lasted approximately one hour.
Participants first completed a shortened complex-span working memory task consisting of Operation Span and Symmetry Span components.
They proceeded to the threestage relational reasoning task.
Participants received standardised instructions and completed a practice question with feedback to ensure that they understood the task requirements.
Before the reasoning task, participants assigned to the incentive condition received standardised information intended to increase the perceived importance of their performance.

They were told that the top-performing third of participants would receive an additional financial bonus, that the Polish results would be compared with results from other European countries, and that they could receive their individual test score.
Participants in the no-incentive condition did not receive these instructions.
Participants then completed the first, chunk-based reasoning stage either with or without access to ChatGPT, depending on the experimental condition.
In the genAIassistance condition, ChatGPT was available on a separate monitor and participants were informed that they could use it freely to support their performance on the task.

At the beginning of the task, participants in this condition were instructed to initiate the ChatGPT conversation by pasting a standardised introductory prompt stating that they were participating in a scientific experiment, and would ask ChatGPT for assistance with various tasks.
Access to ChatGPT was removed before the subsequent network-level reasoning and memory test stages.
After completing the reasoning tasks, participants rated perceived task difficulty and the effort invested in completing the tasks.
They then completed questionnaires concerning their attitudes toward and previous use of generative AI and provided demographic information.
At the end of the session, participants received an initial debriefing explaining the general purpose of the study and the use of partially deceptive instructions.
The full explanation of the motivational manipulation was provided after data collection had been completed to reduce the risk that information about the manipulation would reach future participants.
See Figure 2 for overview of procedure.

text.text: All statistical analyses were conducted using Python and R 4 .
Prior to analysis, assumptions of the respective statistical tests were evaluated, including normality of residuals and homogeneity of variance.
Where necessary, variables were transformed to better satisfy model assumptions; when assumptions remained inadequately met, robust or nonparametric alternatives were used.
Multiple-comparison corrections are reported for the respective analyses.
We distinguish between preregistered hypothesis tests, supporting analyses, and exploratory analyses.
Preregistered hypothesis tests directly addressed the hypotheses specified above.
Supporting analyses were used to characterise task performance, manipulation effects, and other theoretically relevant outcomes that were not direct tests of the preregistered hypotheses.
Exploratory analyses examined additional patterns beyond the primary hypothesis tests and are identified as such throughout the Results.
Results for Stages 1-3 are reported in the chronological order of the experimental procedure.

text.text: >Results
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Results</head>

text.text: The Stage 1 analyses were conducted as supporting analyses to characterise performance during the initial task and the immediate effects of genAI access and performance incentives.
Overall, mean accuracy in Stage 1 was 75.3% (𝑆𝐷 = 14.9%) in the experimental groups.
Mean completion time was 19.5 minutes (𝑀 = 1169 s, 𝑆𝐷 = 395 s).
We conducted a 2 × 2 robust ANOVA to examine the effects of genAI access and performance incentives on Stage 1 accuracy.
We found no significant interaction between genAI access and incentives on accuracy (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.22, 𝑝 = .636, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .001).
There was also no significant main effect of incentives on accuracy (𝐹 (1, 153) = 1.64, 𝑝 = .207, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .011).
However, there was a significant main effect of genAI access on accuracy (𝐹 (1, 153) = 4.71, 𝑝 = .030, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .030).
Participants with access to genAI performed more accurately (𝑀 = 77.85%, 𝑆𝐷 = 14.36%) than participants who worked independently (𝑀 = 72.72%, 𝑆𝐷 = 15.04%; Figure 3).
text.formatted: Participants with access to genAI performed more accurately (𝑀 = 77.85%, 𝑆𝐷 = 14.36%) than participants who worked independently (𝑀 = 72.72%, 𝑆𝐷 = 15.04%; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: We also analysed the difference in performance accuracy between the control condition and the comparable experimental condition (no genAI, no-incentive) to examine whether the two chunked reasoning tasks elicited similar baseline accuracy.
A Mann-Whitney 𝑈 test revealed that there was no difference between the control condition and the comparable experimental condition (𝑈 = 632.5, 𝑝 = .461, 𝑟 rb = -.099).

In an exploratory item-level analysis, to account for individual variability across participants and questions, we also analysed accuracy using a mixed-effects logistic regression (binomial, logit link).
Participants and items were included as random effects, with genAI access, incentives, and their interaction included as fixed effects.
We applied default treatment coding, where the no-genAI, no-incentive condition served as the reference category.
There was no significant effect of genAI access, (𝑏 = 0.268, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.20, 𝑧 = 1.30, 𝑝 = .192), or incentives (𝑏 = 0.128, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.20, 𝑧 = 0.63, 𝑝 = .532).
The interaction between genAI access and incentives was also not significant (𝑏 = 0.136, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.29, 𝑧 = 0.47, 𝑝 = .642).

A 2 × 2 ANOVA on fourth-root-transformed completion times showed that there was no significant interaction between genAI access and incentives (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.41, 𝑝 = .525, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .003), and no significant main effect of genAI access (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.83, 𝑝 = .363, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .005).
However, there was a significant main effect of incentives on completion time (𝐹 (1, 153) = 9.82, 𝑝 = .002, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .060).
Participants in the incentive condition took longer to complete the task (𝑀 = 1262.17 s, 𝑆𝐷 = 390.79 s) than participants in the condition without incentives (𝑀 = 1077.48 s, 𝑆𝐷 = 380.42 s; Figure 4).
text.formatted: Participants in the incentive condition took longer to complete the task (𝑀 = 1262.17 s, 𝑆𝐷 = 390.79 s) than participants in the condition without incentives (𝑀 = 1077.48 s, 𝑆𝐷 = 380.42 s; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>).

text.text: Completion time did not differ significantly between the control condition and the comparable experimental condition (no genAI, no incentives; 𝑡(73) = -0.41, 𝑝 = .684, Cohen's 𝑑 = 0.09).
In an exploratory item-level analysis, we examined completion time using a linear mixed-effects model with treatment coding to account for individual variability across participants and questions.
Participants and items were included as random effects, with genAI access, incentives, and their interaction included as fixed effects.
Fourth-roottransformed completion time was used as the dependent variable.
There was no significant effect of genAI access on completion time (𝑏 = 0.026, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.05, 𝑡(153) = 0.50, 𝑝 = .62).
In contrast, there was a significant effect of incentives (𝑏 = 0.143, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.05, 𝑡(153) = 2.69, 𝑝 = .008).
Under treatment coding, no genAI access was the reference condition.

Within this condition, participants in the no-incentive condition completed the task faster (EMM = 50.49; 95% CI [42.25, 59.88]) than those in the incentive condition (EMM = 59.96; 95% CI [50.56, 70.62]; estimate = -0.117, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.037, 𝑡(153) = -3.131, 𝑝 = .002).
The genAI access × incentives interaction was not significant (𝑏 = -0.051, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.07, 𝑡(153) = -0.684, 𝑝 = .495), providing no evidence that the effect of incentives differed by genAI access.
We analysed the influence of genAI access and incentives on perceived task difficulty in a 2 × 2 ANOVA.

There was no significant interaction between genAI access and incentives (𝐹 (1, 153) = 1.51, 𝑝 = .222, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .010), and no significant main effect of incentives (𝐹 (1, 153) = 1.19, 𝑝 = .276, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .008).
However, there was a significant main effect of genAI access (𝐹 (1, 153) = 5.49, 𝑝 = .020, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .035).
Participants in the no-genAI group reported higher perceived difficulty (𝑀 = 4.71, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.42) than participants in the genAI group (𝑀 = 4.17, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.48; Figure 5).
text.formatted: Participants in the no-genAI group reported higher perceived difficulty (𝑀 = 4.71, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.42) than participants in the genAI group (𝑀 = 4.17, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.48; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref>).

text.text: Perceived task difficulty did not differ significantly between the control condition and the comparable experimental condition (no genAI, no incentives; 𝑈 = 716.5, 𝑝 = .879, 𝑟 rb = .021).
Overall, participants in the experimental groups performed at 61.6% accuracy (𝑆𝐷 = 17.2%) and completed the task in 13.5 minutes (𝑀 = 813 s, 𝑆𝐷 = 319 s).
We performed a 2 × 2 ANOVA to test the preregistered hypotheses regarding effects of prior genAI access and incentives on Stage 2 accuracy.

There was no significant main effect of prior genAI access (𝐹 (1, 153) = 1.84, 𝑝 = .177, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .011), no significant main effect of incentives (𝐹 (1, 153) = 1.14, 𝑝 = .287, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .007), and no significant interaction between prior genAI access and incentives (𝐹 (1, 153) = 2.22, 𝑝 = .138, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .014).
To test the Stage 2 component of H1c, we compared accuracy between the control condition and the comparable experimental condition (no prior genAI access, no incentives).
The difference did not reach statistical significance (𝑡(73) = 1.79, 𝑝 = .078, 𝑑 = 0.41, 95% CI [-0.10, 1.88]).

Participants assigned to the control group showed numerically lower Stage 2 accuracy (𝑀 = 57.3%, 𝑆𝐷 = 17.9%) than participants in the comparable experimental condition with no genAI access and no incentives (𝑀 = 64.1%, 𝑆𝐷 = 15.2%).
Thus, the Stage 2 results were consistent with the direction predicted by H1c, but did not provide statistically significant evidence for the hypothesis.
In an exploratory item-level analysis, we analysed accuracy using a mixed-effects logistic regression (binomial distribution, logit link).
Participants and items were included as random effects, with prior genAI access, incentives, and their interaction included as fixed effects.
Treatment coding was used, with no genAI access and no-incentive as the reference levels.

The genAI × incentive interaction was not significant, indicating no evidence that the association between prior genAI access and accuracy differed between incentive conditions (𝑏 = 0.408, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.277, 𝑧 = 1.47, 𝑝 = .141).
There was also no significant effect of incentives within the no-genAI reference condition (𝑏 = -0.057, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.197, 𝑧 = -0.29, 𝑝 = .770).
Within the no-incentive reference condition, prior genAI access was associated with lower odds of answering a Stage 2 question correctly (𝑏 = -0.392, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.195, 𝑧 = -2.01, 𝑝 = .045, 𝑂𝑅 = 0.68).
Thus, participants who had previously had access to genAI had approximately 32% lower odds of a correct response than participants who had worked without genAI in the noincentive condition.
Because the genAI × incentive interaction was not significant, this conditional effect should not be interpreted as evidence that the effect of genAI differed between incentive conditions (Figure 6).
text.formatted: Because the genAI × incentive interaction was not significant, this conditional effect should not be interpreted as evidence that the effect of genAI differed between incentive conditions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">6</ref>).

text.text: The preregistered analysis of Stage 2 accuracy provided no support for H1a or H1b, as there was no significant main effect of prior genAI access.

The exploratory item-level analysis nevertheless provided some evidence consistent with H1b within the no-incentive condition, where prior genAI access was associated with lower odds of a correct response.
The preregistered effect of incentives on accuracy (H4) was not supported.

A 2 × 2 ANOVA on fourth-root-transformed Stage 2 completion times showed a significant main effect of incentives (𝐹 (1, 153) = 8.44, 𝑝 = .004, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .052), but no significant main effect of prior genAI access (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.30, 𝑝 = .585, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .002).
Participants in the incentive condition took longer to complete the task (𝑀 = 874.6 s, 𝑆𝐷 = 294.4 s) than those in the no-incentive condition (𝑀 = 751.5 s, 𝑆𝐷 = 331.6 s) 5 .
The interaction between prior genAI access and incentives was also significant (𝐹 (1, 153) = 4.38, 𝑝 = .038, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .028).
Post hoc comparisons showed that the effect of incentives was significant among participants without prior genAI access.

Within this group, participants in the no-incentive condition completed the task faster (𝑀 = 707.4 s, 𝑆𝐷 = 266.9 s) than participants in the incentive condition (𝑀 = 941.2 s, 𝑆𝐷 = 281.6 s), 𝑡(76) = 3.72, 𝑝 adj = .002.
There was no difference in completion time between the incentive conditions within the genAI access condition (𝑡(72) = 0.56, 𝑝 adj = .58).

There was also no difference in the completion time between conditions with and without genAI access within the condition with no incentives (𝑡(76) = -0.98, 𝑝 adj = .39) or within the condition with incentives (𝑡(76) = 2.13, 𝑝 adj = .07).
The control group also took significantly longer to complete Stage 2 than the comparable experimental condition (no-genAI, no-incentives; 𝑈 = 435.00, 𝑝 = .005, 𝑟 rb = -.380).
See Figure 7.
text.formatted: See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">7</ref>.

text.text: In an exploratory item-level analysis, we examined fourth-root-transformed completion time per question using a linear mixed-effects regression.
Participants and items were included as random effects, with prior genAI access, incentives, and their interaction included as fixed effects.
A significant prior genAI access × incentives interaction indicated that the effect of incentives depended on prior genAI access condition (𝑏 = -0.191, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.085, 𝑡(153) = -2.253, 𝑝 = .026).

Simple comparisons using emmeans revealed that, in the incentive condition, participants without prior genAI access completed the network-level reasoning task more slowly than those who had initial access to genAI (estimate = 0.140, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.060, 𝑡(153) = 2.328, 𝑝 = .021).
However, there was no significant difference in completion time between the genAI conditions when no additional incentive was provided (estimate = -0.051, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.060, 𝑡(153) = -0.854, 𝑝 = .394).

Further, the effect of incentives was significant among participants without genAI access, such that participants completed the task more slowly when additional incentives were provided (EMM = 54.30; 95%CI[44.03; 66.28]) than when no additional incentives were provided (EMM = 39.00; 95%CI [31.04; 48.40]; estimate = -0.216, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.060, 𝑡(153) = -3.584, 𝑝 < .001).
text.formatted: Further, the effect of incentives was significant among participants without genAI access, such that participants completed the task more slowly when additional incentives were provided (EMM = 54.30; 95%CI[44.03; 66.28]) than when no additional incentives were provided (EMM = 39.00; 95%CI [31.04; 48.40]; estimate = -0.216, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.060, 𝑡(153) = -3.584, 𝑝 < .001).

text.text: In contrast, there was no significant difference between the incentive conditions among participants with genAI access (estimate = -0.025, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.060, 𝑡(153) = -0.410, 𝑝 = .682).
In a further exploratory analysis, we examined whether the effects of prior genAI access and incentives on completion time varied with question difficulty.
Question difficulty was operationalised as the proportion of incorrect responses to each question across all participants.

We conducted a second linear mixed-effects regression with participants and items as random effects, and fixed effects of prior genAI access, incentives, and question difficulty, as well as their interactions.
The model showed a significant three-way interaction between prior genAI access, incentive and question difficulty (𝑏 = -0.51, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.24, 𝑡(1869) = -2.08, 𝑝 = .038).
Follow-up analyses indicated that the genAI × incentives interaction varied as a function of question difficulty.

The interaction was not significant at low question difficulty (1 𝑆𝐷 below the mean; 𝑏 = 0.514, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.349, 𝑡(2014) = 1.47, 𝑝 = .142) or at the mean level of question difficulty (𝑏 = 0.008, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.128, 𝑡(701) = 0.07, 𝑝 = .948), but was significant at high question difficulty (1 𝑆𝐷 above the mean; 𝑏 = -0.497, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.170, 𝑡(1413) = -2.93, 𝑝 = .004).
We therefore examined simple effects at high question difficulty.
Among participants without incentives, question completion time did not differ significantly between the genAI and no-genAI conditions (estimate = -0.178, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.120, 𝑡(1413) = -1.49, 𝑝 = .138).

In contrast, among participants who received additional incentives, completion times were significantly longer in the no-genAI condition (EMM noAI = 126.4 s, 95%𝐶𝐼[73.2, 204.5]) than in the genAI condition (EMM AI = 84.7 s, 95%𝐶𝐼[46.1; 143.7], estimate = 0.319, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.120, 𝑡(1413) = 2.65, 𝑝 = .008).
Examining the simple effects of incentives produced a complementary pattern.

Among participants without access to genAI, completion time was significantly faster in the no-incentive condition (EMM = 81.8, 95% CI [44.2, 139.3]) than in the incentive condition (EMM = 126.4, 95% CI [73.1, 204.5], estimate = -0.346, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.12, 𝑡(1413) = -2.87, 𝑝 = .004).
Among participants with access to genAI, there was no difference in completion time, regardless of incentives (estimate = 0.151, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.12, 𝑡(1413) = 1.26, 𝑝 = .208).
The three-way interaction is illustrated in Figure 8.
text.formatted: The three-way interaction is illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">8</ref>.

text.text: For completion time, there was no significant main effect of prior genAI access, providing no support for H2a or H2b.
Completion time differed as a function of incentives, supporting H5, with participants in the incentive condition taking longer overall.

Further analyses indicated that this effect depended on prior genAI access and question difficulty: incentives were associated with greater time investment particularly on difficult questions among participants without prior genAI access.
We analysed the influence of prior genAI access and incentives on perceived task difficulty in a 2 × 2 ANOVA.

There was no effect of prior genAI access (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.21, 𝑝 = .646, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .001) or incentives (𝐹 (1, 153) = 2.70, 𝑝 = .102, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .017) on task difficulty, and no significant interaction (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.35, 𝑝 = .557, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .002).

Participants who were assigned to the control group reported slightly higher task difficulty (𝑀 = 5.44, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.25), compared to the experimental group (𝑀 = 4.97, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.25), but the difference was not significant (𝑈 = 531.50, 𝑝 = .061, 𝑟 rb = -0.24).
>Stage 3: Memory Performance
text.formatted: <head n="3.3." >Stage 3: Memory Performance</head>

text.text: Overall performance on the memory test was 𝑀 = 57.5%, 𝑆𝐷 = 17.6%.
We conducted a 2 × 2 ANOVA to test the preregistered effects of prior genAI access and incentives on memory performance.
There was no significant main effect of prior genAI access (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.095, 𝑝 = .758, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .001) and no significant main effect of incentives (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.022, 𝑝 = .882, 𝜂 2 𝑝 < .001).
text.formatted: There was no significant main effect of prior genAI access (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.095, 𝑝 = .758, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .001) and no significant main effect of incentives (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.022, 𝑝 = .882, 𝜂 2 𝑝 < .001).

text.text: The exploratory interaction between prior genAI access and incentives was also not significant (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.108, 𝑝 = .743, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .001).
Thus, the analysis provided no support for H3.
To test the Stage 3 component of H1c, we compared memory performance between the control condition and the comparable experimental condition (no prior genAI access, no incentives).
There was no significant difference between the conditions (𝑡(73) = 0.045, 𝑝 = .964, 𝑑 = 0.01, 95% CI [-0.83, 0.87]).
Thus, the Stage 3 results provided no support for H1c.

A two-way robust ANOVA revealed no significant main effect of prior genAI access, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.37, 𝑝 = .542, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .002, and no significant main effect of incentives, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 3.07, 𝑝 = .082, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .020.
However, there was a significant genAI × incentives interaction, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 5.04, 𝑝 = .0262, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .032.

Post hoc comparisons revealed that, among participants with prior genAI access, those in the incentive condition reported higher task difficulty (𝑀 = 6.10, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.19) than those in the no-incentive condition (𝑀 = 5.79, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.41; 𝑡(72.07) = -2.84, 𝑝 adj = .035, 𝑑 = -0.64).
There was no significant difference between incentive conditions among participants without prior genAI access (𝑡(76) = -0.50, 𝑝 adj = .62).

There was also no significant difference between participants with and without prior genAI access within the incentive condition (𝑡(76) = -1.93, 𝑝 adj = .17) or within the no-incentive condition (𝑡(77) = 1.34, 𝑝 adj = .31; Figure 9).
text.formatted: There was also no significant difference between participants with and without prior genAI access within the incentive condition (𝑡(76) = -1.93, 𝑝 adj = .17) or within the no-incentive condition (𝑡(77) = 1.34, 𝑝 adj = .31; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">9</ref>).

text.text: Perceived task difficulty did not differ significantly between the control condition and the comparable experimental condition (no prior genAI access, no incentive; 𝑈 = 644.5, 𝑝 = .507, 𝑟 rb = -.082).

To test whether performance incentives influenced cognitive offloading among participants with access to genAI, we compared the number of genAI queries submitted by participants in the incentive and no-incentive conditions.
A Mann-Whitney 𝑈 test revealed no significant difference between the two conditions (𝑈 = 664.0, 𝑝 = .334, 𝑟 rb = -.126).
Thus, H6, which predicted greater cognitive offloading in the no-incentive condition, was not supported.
We conducted a linear regression to examine whether working memory capacity predicted the number of genAI queries submitted during Stage 1.
Because the residuals deviated from normality, robust standard errors were used.
The overall model was not significant (𝐹 (1, 76) = 0.01, 𝑝 = .903, 𝑅 2 < .001, adjusted 𝑅2 = -.013).
text.formatted: The overall model was not significant (𝐹 (1, 76) = 0.01, 𝑝 = .903, 𝑅 2 < .001, adjusted 𝑅2 = -.013).

text.text: Working memory capacity was not a significant predictor of the number of genAI queries (𝑏 = .008, 𝑆𝐸 = .061, 𝑡(76) = 0.122, 𝑝 = .903, 95% CI [-.114, .129]).
Thus, H7, which predicted greater cognitive offloading among participants with lower working memory capacity, was not supported.

text.text: We examined self-reported effort using the Effort/Importance subscale of the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (Deci et al., 1994).
text.formatted: We examined self-reported effort using the Effort/Importance subscale of the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Deci et al., 1994)</ref>.

text.text: A two-way robust ANOVA showed no significant main effect of genAI access (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.29, 𝑝 = .59, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .001) and no significant main effect of incentives (𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.21, 𝑝 = .65, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .001).
However, the interaction between genAI access and incentives was significant (𝐹 (1, 153) = 4.34, 𝑝 = .039, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .028).
Post hoc comparisons showed no significant simple effects after correction for multiple comparisons.

Among participants without genAI access, self-reported effort was numerically higher in the incentive condition than in the no-incentive condition, but this difference did not remain significant after correction (𝑈 = 1003.5, 𝑝 = .088, Hedges' 𝑔 = 0.40; Figure 10).
text.formatted: Among participants without genAI access, self-reported effort was numerically higher in the incentive condition than in the no-incentive condition, but this difference did not remain significant after correction (𝑈 = 1003.5, 𝑝 = .088, Hedges' 𝑔 = 0.40; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_9">10</ref>).

text.text: Self-reported effort did not differ significantly between the control condition and the comparable experimental condition (no genAI access, no incentives; 𝑈 = 522.0, 𝑝 = .056, 𝑟 rb = -.256).
We examined participants' self-reported frequency of genAI tools usage, as well as their attitudes towards genAI (measured with AIAS-4, Grassini (2023); (Juranek & Pochwatko, 2026)).

text.text: A two-way robust ANOVA revealed no significant main effect of genAI access on usage frequency, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.15, 𝑝 = .701, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .001, no significant main effect of incentives, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.67, 𝑝 = .413, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .004, and no significant interaction between genAI and incentives, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 2.15, 𝑝 = .140, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .014.

A 2 × 2 ANOVA revealed no significant main effect of genAI access on self-reported attitudes towards AI, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.24, 𝑝 = .625, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .002, no significant main effect of incentives, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.01, 𝑝 = .913, 𝜂 2 𝑝 < .001, and no significant interaction between genAI access and incentives, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 1.97, 𝑝 = .162, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .013.
text.formatted: A 2 × 2 ANOVA revealed no significant main effect of genAI access on self-reported attitudes towards AI, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.24, 𝑝 = .625, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .002, no significant main effect of incentives, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 0.01, 𝑝 = .913, 𝜂 2 𝑝 < .001, and no significant interaction between genAI access and incentives, 𝐹 (1, 153) = 1.97, 𝑝 = .162, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .013.

text.text: In an exploratory analysis, we examined how participants used ChatGPT during the Stage 1 chunk-based reasoning task and whether different patterns of use were associated with task performance.
We classified the conversations conducted during Stage 1.
The coding captured two types of information.
First, at the item level, we recorded the number of task items for which each participant consulted ChatGPT.
Second, at the participant level, we classified each participant according to their overall pattern of ChatGPT use.
The classification scheme was developed inductively based on an initial review of the conversations by three researchers.
Subsequently, two other researchers independently classified all conversations into one of four mutually exclusive categories.
Inter-rater agreement was Cohen's 𝜅 = 0.85, indicating almost perfect agreement.
The coders resolved all disagreements through discussion and assigned a final category by consensus.
The four categories were as follows: 1.
No or occasional use: Participants did not use Chat-GPT or exchanged no more than three messages with it.
Question copying: Participants copied and pasted task items into ChatGPT without adding substantive comments or follow-up questions.

Exploratory use: Participants engaged with ChatGPT beyond merely submitting task items, for example by proposing their own answers, requesting justification, asking follow-up questions, or expressing disagreement with the chatbot's responses.
Other use: Participants used ChatGPT primarily for purposes unrelated to obtaining or discussing answers, for example as a notepad.
Of the 79 participants in the genAI condition, one could not be included in the analysis because their conversation was not saved.

Among the remaining 78 participants, 31 were classified as showing no or only occasional use, 28 as engaging in question copying, 16 as engaging in exploratory use, and 3 as using ChatGPT in other ways.
Because the last category was both small and heterogeneous, these three participants were excluded from subsequent comparisons between patterns of ChatGPT use.
Thus, the following analyses compared the three main groups (𝑁 = 75).
The groups differed significantly in Stage 1 accuracy, 𝐹 (2, 72) = 3.15, 𝑝 = .049, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .080.
Mean accuracy was 74.4% in the no-or-occasional-use group, 81.7% in the question-copying group, and 82.3% in the exploratory-use group.
Tukey's HSD post hoc tests indicated that none of the pairwise differences reached statistical significance (𝑝s = .079-.990).
Kruskal-Wallis test revealed that the genAI use-type groups also differed significantly in the time required to complete the Stage 1 task, 𝐻(2) = 6.31, 𝑝 = .043, 𝜖2 = .060.
The mean completion times were 1148 s in the no-oroccasional-use group, 1137 s in the question-copying group, and 1473 s in the exploratory-use group.

Pairwise Mann-Whitney 𝑈 tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction indicated that participants in the exploratory-use group spent more time on the task than participants in both the no-oroccasional-use group (𝑝 adj = .041) and the question-copying group (𝑝 adj = .041).
The latter two groups did not differ significantly (𝑝 adj = .897).
The groups also differed in their attitudes toward AI, 𝐹 (2, 72) = 6.27, 𝑝 = .003, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = .148.
The mean attitude scores were 4.42 in the no-or-occasional-use group, 6.10 in the question-copying group, and 6.52 in the exploratory-use group.

Tukey's HSD post hoc tests showed that participants in the no-or-occasional-use group reported less favorable attitudes toward artificial intelligence than participants in both the question-copying group (𝑝 = .014) and the exploratoryuse group (𝑝 = .009).
The latter two groups did not differ significantly (𝑝 = .823).
These groups also differed in perceived Stage 1 task difficulty, 𝐻(2) = 6.94, 𝑝 = .031, 𝜖2 = .069.
Participants in the no-or-occasional-use group reported greater task difficulty than those in the question-copying group (𝑝 adj = .035).
The remaining pairwise comparisons were not statistically significant (𝑝 adj = .145 and .721).

No statistically significant differences between the genAI use-type groups were found in working-memory capacity, 𝐹 (2, 72) = 1.44, 𝑝 = .244; Stage 2 completion time, 𝐻(2) = 0.92, 𝑝 = .631; Stage 2 accuracy, 𝐹 (2, 72) = 1.29, 𝑝 = .281; Stage 3 memory-test performance, 𝐻(2) = 3.80, 𝑝 = .150; self-reported effort, 𝐻(2) = 4.88, 𝑝 = .087; Stage 2 perceived difficulty, 𝐻(2) = 5.41, 𝑝 = .067; or Stage 3 perceived difficulty, 𝐻(2) = 1.26, 𝑝 = .532.

Among participants who used ChatGPT, Stage 1 accuracy was positively associated with the number of queries submitted to ChatGPT (Spearman's 𝑟 𝑠 = .376, 𝑝 < .001), indicating that participants who interacted with ChatGPT more frequently tended to achieve higher accuracy in the chunked reasoning task.
text.formatted: Among participants who used ChatGPT, Stage 1 accuracy was positively associated with the number of queries submitted to ChatGPT (Spearman's 𝑟 𝑠 = .376, 𝑝 < .001), indicating that participants who interacted with ChatGPT more frequently tended to achieve higher accuracy in the chunked reasoning task.

text.text: Finally, at the item level, question difficulty, operationalized as the proportion of incorrect responses to each item, was positively correlated with the number of participants who referred to that item in their conversations with Chat-GPT, 𝑟(16) = .607, 𝑝 = .008.
Thus, more difficult items were discussed with ChatGPT by a greater number of participants.
The present study examined how prior genAI use shapes subsequent independent reasoning within an interconnected network of information.
After initially working with or without genAI support, participants were required to reason independently about relations distributed across the same broader knowledge network.
Access to genAI provided immediate benefits during the assisted task, including higher aggregate accuracy and lower perceived difficulty.

However, these benefits did not clearly transfer to subsequent independent performance: item-level analyses indicated poorer reasoning after prior genAI use, which suggests that it might have altered the process of relational learning.
Prior genAI use was also associated with altered effort regulation, as participants showed a weaker increase in effort in response to incentives, particularly for more difficult questions.
The present findings suggest a trade-off between the immediate benefits of genAI assistance and the subsequent ability to reason independently about the same relational structure.

During the initial chunk-based reasoning task, participants with access to genAI achieved higher aggregate accuracy and perceived the task as less difficult than participants who worked independently.
Performance incentives, in contrast, increased completion time without producing a corresponding increase in accuracy.
Thus, genAI facilitated performance on the immediate task, whereas incentives primarily increased the amount of time participants were willing to invest.

This immediate benefit is consistent with a cognitiveoffloading account, according to which external tools can reduce the internal processing demands of a task (Risko & Gilbert, 2016; Skulmowski, 2023).
text.formatted: This immediate benefit is consistent with a cognitiveoffloading account, according to which external tools can reduce the internal processing demands of a task <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Risko & Gilbert, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Skulmowski, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, this interpretation is further supported by participants' actual use of genAI: those who submitted more queries to ChatGPT tended to achieve higher Stage 1 accuracy, and more difficult questions were more likely to prompt genAI use.
Participants therefore appeared to turn to genAI particularly when cognitive demands were high, and doing so was associated with better immediate performance.
The more important question was whether these benefits transferred to subsequent independent reasoning.
However, at the aggregate level, prior genAI access did not significantly affect Stage 2 accuracy.
The item-level mixed-effects analysis provided some evidence of poorer subsequent reasoning following genAI use.
Within the no-incentive reference condition, prior genAI access was associated with lower odds of answering individual Stage 2 questions correctly.
Because the genAI × incentive interaction was not significant, this conditional effect should be interpreted cautiously.

Nevertheless, the direction of this result is consistent with the interpretation that genAI assistance reduced the construction of relational knowledge needed later, that is, it disrupted the knowledge acquisition process.
In Stage 1, participants had to identify relevant information and integrate relations across multiple statements.
These operations were not only necessary for answering the immediate questions, but also for constructing a representation of the broader relational network.
If genAI performed part of this integration, participants could obtain a correct answer while engaging less deeply with the structure underlying it.

This interpretation is consistent with previous work showing that more effortful, self-generated processing can support learning of deeper problem structure and later transfer (O'Hara & Payne, 1998), as well as with more recent findings suggesting that genAI assistance can improve immediate performance without necessarily producing equivalent gains in knowledge acquisition or transfer (Fan et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with previous work showing that more effortful, self-generated processing can support learning of deeper problem structure and later transfer <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(O'Hara & Payne, 1998)</ref>, as well as with more recent findings suggesting that genAI assistance can improve immediate performance without necessarily producing equivalent gains in knowledge acquisition or transfer <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fan et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The control condition provides additional context for interpreting the Stage 2 results.

In Stage 1, the control task was comparable to the baseline condition (no genAI, no incentive) in accuracy, completion time, and perceived difficulty, but control participants did not acquire prior knowledge of the relational network used in Stage 2.
Despite this lack of relevant prior knowledge, their Stage 2 accuracy did not differ significantly from that of the baseline experimental group.
Instead, control participants spent significantly more time completing the task.

In other words, differences in prior knowledge between the control and baseline conditions were not necessarily reflected in aggregate Stage 2 accuracy, but control participants may have compensated for their lack of prior knowledge by investing more time in reconstructing the relevant relations from the information available during Stage 2.
No effects of prior genAI access or incentives emerged in the Stage 3 memory test.
This result limits how strongly the Stage 2 findings can be interpreted as evidence of impaired learning.
Importantly, the memory test assessed information encountered across both Stage 1 and Stage 2.
Participants therefore had an additional opportunity to process the relevant information independently before memory was tested.
The absence of group differences in Stage 3 may indicate that subsequent independent exposure reduced earlier differences in knowledge acquisition.
It may also reflect a distinction between remembering individual pieces of information and being able to use their relational structure to derive new conclusions.

Taken together, the findings suggest that genAI helped participants solve the immediate reasoning task, particularly when cognitive demands were high, but these benefits did not clearly transfer to later independent reasoning.

The results are consistent with the interpretation that when genAI performs some of the integration required by a task, users may engage less deeply in constructing the relational knowledge needed later.
More broadly, this supports the distinction between using genAI to support cognitive processing and using it to replace processing that is itself important for learning (Lo et al., 2024).
text.formatted: More broadly, this supports the distinction between using genAI to support cognitive processing and using it to replace processing that is itself important for learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Lo et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the present task, information integration was both a source of difficulty and a central part of what participants needed to learn.

From the educational perspective, the findings raise the possibility that successful completion of genAI-assisted tasks may not reliably reflect the learners' ability to independently integrate and apply the underlying information.
GenAI use altered subsequent effort regulation, particularly by weakening the effect of external incentives when task demands were high.
This pattern was already visible at the group level.
Participants in the incentive condition without prior genAI access spent more time on Stage 2 than the no-genAI, no-incentive baseline group.
Participants in the control condition also spent more time on Stage 2 than the baseline group, despite receiving no incentive and having no prior knowledge of the relevant network from Stage 1.

Their longer completion time may therefore reflect compensatory effort: because they could not rely on previously acquired network knowledge, they devoted more time to processing the information available in Stage 2.
By contrast, neither group with prior genAI access showed a similar increase in time investment.
This suggests that prior genAI use reduced participants' tendency to increase effort when additional effort could have been useful.
The item-level analysis provides the clearest evidence for this interpretation.
The interaction between prior genAI use, incentives, and question difficulty showed that differences in time allocation were concentrated among the most difficult questions.
In the no-genAI condition, incentives increased the time devoted to difficult questions.
This adjustment was much weaker among participants who had previously completed Stage 1 with genAI assistance.
Prior genAI use therefore did not reduce time investment equally across all questions.
Instead, it weakened incentive-sensitive effort mobilisation when task demands were high.
This pattern cannot be explained by participants experiencing Stage 2 as unusually difficult after losing access to genAI.
Although participants with genAI access rated Stage 1 as easier than those who worked independently, perceived difficulty in Stage 2 did not differ across the experimental conditions.
The reduced adjustment of effort among prior genAI users therefore occurred without a corresponding increase in their reported task difficulty.
One possible explanation can be derived from motivation intensity theory.

According to this framework, effort increases with task difficulty only while success remains possible and the required effort does not exceed the maximum effort justified by the importance of success, referred to as potential motivation (Brehm et al., 1983).
text.formatted: According to this framework, effort increases with task difficulty only while success remains possible and the required effort does not exceed the maximum effort justified by the importance of success, referred to as potential motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brehm et al., 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Prior genAI use may have lowered the amount of personal effort that participants considered justified for this task.
As a result, difficult questions may have reached this subjective limit sooner.

Participants without prior genAI access continued to increase their effort when an incentive made successful performance more important, whereas participants with prior genAI access did not show the same increase.
The self-reported effort results were broadly consistent with this account.
There was a significant interaction between genAI use and incentives, but none of the simple comparisons were significant.
Numerically, incentives were associated with greater declared effort among participants who had worked without genAI, whereas the pattern was reversed among participants with prior genAI access.

Thus, the behavioural effect was accompanied by a similar descriptive pattern in participants' reports: those who had used genAI responded faster and reported relatively less effort when an incentive was present.
In simpler terms, successful performance with genAI during Stage 1 may have suggested that the task could be completed with relatively little personal effort.
Participants may then have judged a high level of independent effort as less worthwhile when the tool was no longer available.
This does not necessarily mean that genAI reduced their general motivation or interest.
Rather, it may have lowered the amount of effort they considered reasonable to invest in this particular task.
A second explanation concerns altered effort calibration.

From the expected value of control perspective, the amount of cognitive control allocated to a task depends on the expected benefits of control, its expected effect on performance, and its subjective costs (Shenhav et al., 2013).
text.formatted: From the expected value of control perspective, the amount of cognitive control allocated to a task depends on the expected benefits of control, its expected effect on performance, and its subjective costs <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Shenhav et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: During Stage 1, genAI improved performance and reduced perceived difficulty.

Participants may therefore have learned an inaccurate relation between personal effort and successful performance: good performance appeared possible with relatively little internally generated processing.

When genAI was removed in Stage 2, they may have failed to adjust this estimate to the greater demands of unaided reasoning and consequently allocated too little time and control, especially to difficult questions.
The two explanations differ in an important respect.
Under the potential-motivation account, participants may have recognised that additional effort could improve performance but nevertheless treated that effort as not worth its cost.
This judgment need not have been fully conscious.
Under the calibration account, they may instead have underestimated how much personal effort was required or how strongly additional effort would improve performance.

The interaction in self-reported effort makes the potential-motivation account somewhat more plausible, because participants' reports followed the same general pattern as their behaviour, suggesting that they were at least partly aware of investing less effort.
However, because none of the simple effects were significant, the evidence does not clearly distinguish between the two mechanisms.
They may also have operated together.
Both accounts describe a change in effort regulation rather than a simple decline in reasoning ability.
The findings also do not support a simple explanation in which genAI use made participants overlook or forget the incentive instructions.
The incentive increased completion time during Stage 1, indicating that participants responded to the manipulation even when genAI was available.
Moreover, participants in the control condition, who received no incentive, nevertheless spent more time on Stage 2 than the baseline group.
An explicit reward was therefore not necessary for greater time investment.

Instead, prior experience of solving Stage 1 independently may have supported a higher level of later effort mobilisation, whereas genAI-assisted performance may have reduced the amount of independent effort that appeared necessary or justified.
Taken together, these findings suggest that prior genAI use changed how participants allocated effort after the tool was removed.
Participants who had previously worked independently increased their effort when incentives and task difficulty made additional investment useful.
Participants who had used genAI showed a weaker adjustment.
This pattern may reflect a lower level of potential motivation, inaccurate calibration of the effort required for unaided performance, or a combination of both processes.

For learning activities that alternate between AI-supported and independent work, this raises the question of whether learners also need support in recalibrating the effort they expect to invest once assistance is withdrawn.
Contrary to our predictions, cognitive offloading was not systematically related to either working memory capacity or performance incentives.
Working memory capacity did not predict the number of queries participants submitted to genAI.
Similarly, additional performance incentives did not increase or decrease the number of genAI queries.

Thus, having fewer internal cognitive resources did not appear to make participants more likely to rely on the external tool, and increasing the importance of successful performance was not sufficient to change the extent to which they used it.
Instead, participants' attitudes towards genAI were more clearly associated with whether and how they engaged with the available tool.
This pattern was particularly apparent in the qualitative analysis of ChatGPT-use behaviour.
Almost 40% of participants with access to genAI either did not use ChatGPT at all or used it only occasionally.
These participants reported substantially less favourable attitudes toward genAI than those who used genAI in the task.
This pattern was observed despite all participants having the same opportunity to use the tool.
A substantial proportion of participants effectively chose to continue solving the task internally.
The behavioural categories further suggest that cognitive offloading should not be treated as a unitary behaviour.

Among participants who reported using genAI regularly, 28 primarily copied task questions to ChatGPT, whereas 16 engaged in more exploratory interactions, such as proposing their own answers, requesting explanations, asking followup questions, or challenging the model's responses.
These strategies imply different degrees of cognitive delegation.

Question copying represents a relatively direct transfer of problem solving to the external system, whereas exploratory use retains greater involvement of the participant in evaluating and integrating the generated information.
A simple count of queries therefore captures the amount of interaction with genAI but does not fully characterise the cognitive processes being offloaded.

The exploratory use group also spent substantially more time on Stage 1 than either the question-copying or no-oroccasional-use groups, while the two groups that decided to use ChatGPT achieved numerically higher accuracy.
This pattern suggests that genAI use need not necessarily function as an effort-reduction strategy.
For some participants, particularly those using the tool exploratorily, genAI became an additional resource with which they actively interacted rather than a substitute for task engagement.
The item-level analysis also showed that participants were more likely to turn to genAI when they encountered more difficult questions.

This pattern is consistent with the role of element interactivity proposed by cognitive load theory: questions that require more information to be maintained and integrated simultaneously impose greater demands on working memory and may therefore increase the value of external cognitive support.
Interestingly, although working memory capacity did not predict overall genAI use across participants, question difficulty predicted when participants were more likely to seek assistance.
This suggests that offloading in the present task may have been more sensitive to the cognitive demands of a particular problem than to stable individual differences in working memory capacity.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the present findings.
First, the evidence that prior genAI use impaired subsequent relational reasoning was not fully consistent across levels of analysis.

In the network-level reasoning task, the analysis of aggregated accuracy scores did not reveal a significant main effect of genAI assistance, whereas the negative effect emerged in the item-level mixedeffects analysis.
This suggests that the effect may be modest and sensitive to the analytical approach and individual variability between participants and items.
Moreover, there was no significant interaction between genAI assistance and performance incentives on accuracy.
These findings should therefore be interpreted cautiously and replicated in future studies using larger samples or stronger incentives.
A related limitation concerns variation in actual genAI use.
Providing access to ChatGPT did not necessarily result in substantial cognitive offloading, as some participants did not use the tool or used it only occasionally.
This may have reduced differences between the genAI and no-genAI conditions.
Future studies should therefore distinguish between access to genAI and the extent or type of cognitive offloading.
Second, performance incentives did not increase accuracy, although they affected the time participants devoted to the tasks.
This suggests that the manipulation influenced effort allocation without necessarily improving performance.
It remains unclear whether this reflects a limitation of the manipulation or of the task itself.
Participants may already have been highly motivated in the no-incentive condition, leaving limited room for improvement.
In addition, completion time is only an indirect measure of effort.
Future studies should therefore include additional behavioural and subjective measures of effort.
A further limitation concerns the operationalisation of question difficulty in the exploratory analyses.

Because difficulty was estimated from item-level accuracy in the present sample, the observed moderation effect should be interpreted cautiously and possibly replicated using independently established estimates of question difficulty.
Finally, the present incentive manipulation primarily targeted extrinsic motivation and therefore does not allow conclusions about how genAI interacts with intrinsic motivation.
Future research should examine whether factors such as task interest, perceived competence, autonomy, and personal relevance influence cognitive engagement when genAI support is available.

Overall, the results showed that while use of genAI made participants perform better and perceive the task as less difficult, it also influenced effort regulation on subsequent tasks and dampened the effects of motivational incentives.
The findings are in line with previous studies suggesting that relying on genAI for cognitive tasks may have detrimental effect on learning and self-regulation mechanisms.
Additionally, we found that participants' choice to rely on genAI depended both on question difficulty as well as their prior frequency of use and attitudes towards genAI.
As the genAI technology becomes more prevalent, these findings highlight opportunities for future studies on motivational factors in human-genAI interaction.
